_about: Full-episode-only keys for scenarios/awareness_e16_insider_risk/scenario.json.erb (the E16 full shell). The wiring agent pastes each value into the full erb at the path its _notes line gives. None of these is carried into the generated defend-only shell by gen_e8_e17_shells.py EXCEPT concernForm: it is a DEFEND_HALF_KEY, so gen_e8_e17_shells.py defend_half_keys() copies it from this file into the defend-only shell too (E16 section 13); the sandbox and the montage stay full-only. Authored by opus48. ENG-04 (mistake stage + montage flip), ENG-12 (concernForm) and ENG-08 (schema) have landed. TONE (E16 section 18, a blocker): no blame, no surveillance framing; the flip ends on the kind, fair Samira outcome, and the concern form favours facts over a verdict.

_notes.mistake: Paste at social.awarenessEpisode.mistake (ENG-04). The five everyday choices of the leaver's week, in authored order. Exactly one safe:true option per beat; the safe option's position is varied beat to beat (2nd, 2nd, 2nd, 1st, 2nd; only leaver_favour lists the safe option first, per ENG-04) so it is never always first. F-E16-2 (E16_BLIND_B1 item 2): the safe option used to be the long, hedged one every time, so a skimmer could pick by length alone; the labels are now balanced in length (the longer option is the unsafe one in some beats, the safe one in others, and equal in others) and the 'if ... otherwise' hedges are gone, so neither length nor position gives the answer away. F-E16-3 (E16_BLIND_B4 item 3): the risky option used to be the obvious favour/direct/theory one every time; two now read as plausible, well-meant steps (outside_offer 'engage' is the instinct to find out who is behind it, samira 'confront' is giving her a chance to clear it up) so the safe answer is not always the obvious 'proper channel' one. flipBeat is outside_offer (the one consequential choice quoted first in the montage). beats are authored shared_login, rumour, outside_offer, leaver_favour, samira so that the montage (flipBeat first, then the rest in authored order) ENDS on the samira beat's kind resolution. Never scored. Full-only: dropped from the defend-only shell with the mistake stage.

beats.situation: Reuben is locked out with a report due at ten. "Can I just use yours? Two minutes."

options.label: Let him use your login while you sit beside him
Send him to the service desk to get a reset

beats.situation: At lunch, Craig floats that Samira is leaving with Ross and taking the client list.

options.label: Say you'd wondered about her leaving too
Suggest he takes it to security or his manager

beats.situation: An unknown contact messages you: "We pay people at firms like yours for remote access. 25% of what we make. Totally anonymous. Interested?"

options.label: Reply to find out who's really behind it
Screenshot it and send it to security

beats.situation: Ross asks you to export his accounts to his personal email "for the handover".

options.label: Check with his manager what the handover needs
Export the accounts to his personal email as asked

beats.situation: Samira has been in early, taking calls in the stairwell, and visiting HR.

options.label: Ask her straight so she can clear it up
Ask how her week is going and leave it at that

outside_offer.engage: A reply drew more pressure, then a flood of sign-in prompts that night. The same message had gone to several people; the one who reported it warned everyone.
outside_offer.report: The version where someone replied instead: the pressure grew and the sign-in prompts came that night. Reporting it, without a word back, stopped it and warned the team. You are not in trouble for being approached.

shared_login.log_in_for_him: Reuben clicked the wrong shortcut and opened the HR drive, under your name, on the record until it was explained. Harmless this time; a reset would have cost two minutes.
shared_login.service_desk: The version where a login was shared: whatever was opened went on the record of whoever's login it was. The service desk reset it in minutes instead.

rumour.add: Your remark reached Samira, who had been at the hospital every night. It wasn't true, and it landed on someone already having the worst week.
rumour.route: The version where the theory spread: it reached Samira, and it wasn't true. Facts to the right person help; a theory in the kitchen only hurts.

leaver_favour.personal_email: The client list sat in a personal inbox outside the firm. Company data belongs to the company, and the people in it belong to themselves.
leaver_favour.handover: The version where accounts went to a personal inbox: the firm's data left its protection. Handover notes agreed with his manager and kept in the shared place did the job and kept the data in.

samira.confront: Samira, whose father was in hospital, was asked whether she was leaving with Ross. She wasn't. The question made a hard week harder.
samira.kind: A kind word, and nothing more: Samira's father was in hospital, and she told you when she was ready. Nobody was accused, and she got support from the people she chose. That is what good looks like.

defendIntro: That's where this week's choices led. Now a fair way to raise a concern, facts, not a verdict on anyone, and then a short set of messages. Take them at your own pace.

factChips.label: An unknown contact offered payment for remote access
The message came on Tuesday evening
Through a messaging app, from the handle 'Opportunities'
It came to me; I gather others were messaged too
A colleague has seemed to be having a hard week
A colleague on my team; I'd rather not say more than that

conclusionChips.label: Ross is stealing the client list
Samira is in on it with Ross

concernForm.guidance: Put anything offered to you, like an approach for access, in the report; a worry about a colleague's wellbeing is not something for a security report, so raise that with your manager or HR. Who to tell: the security team for an outside offer, a sign-in prompt you didn't start, or data or access being misused. If it involves personal data, tell the data protection officer. Posting it in the team chat is spreading it, not raising it.

strings.title: Raise a concern
strings._launch: F-E16-4 (E15_E16_PLAYTEST_P1, E16_BLIND_B1 item 4): the form runs before the inbox in BOTH variants (concern-form-minigame.js). In the full shell the learner has just played the week's choices; in the defend-only shell it is the first thing they see, so the engine default launch text ('build a short report from what you noticed') lands cold, and the blind run found the conclusion chips named Ross, Samira and Craig with no introduction. launchText now names all three and the offer in a couple of lines so both the fact chips and the conclusion chips make sense cold, in either run (episode-model.js CONCERN_LAUNCH override).
strings.launchText: This week an unknown contact offered you money for access. A colleague, Samira, has seemed to be having a hard week, and at lunch Craig floated a theory that she and Ross, a leaver, are walking off with the client list. Build a short report of what you actually saw, as facts, not a verdict on anyone.
strings.intro: Write it as facts you saw yourself, not a verdict on anyone. Anything offered to you, like this approach for access, belongs in the report; a worry about a colleague's wellbeing is one for your manager or HR instead. Pick the facts to put in the report.
strings.feedbackFacts: Good. Facts, not a verdict, are what a fair concern looks like. Anything offered to you belongs in a report like this; a worry about a colleague's wellbeing goes to your manager or HR instead. The note below says who to tell. You don't have to be sure, and you may not hear the outcome, because that's confidential too.
strings.feedbackFactsVerdict: You have facts in there, which is the right idea. A conclusion about a person does not belong in the report: take those picks out, and let whoever looks into it reach their own. Keep anything offered to you in; a worry about a colleague's wellbeing is one for your manager or HR, not this report. That's fairer to everyone, and you don't have to be sure to raise a fair concern.
strings.feedbackVerdictOnly: That's a conclusion, not something you saw, and it does not belong in the report. Take it out and leave the verdict to the people whose job and lawful process it is; give them what you actually noticed instead. If you're wrong, a verdict is unfair to someone who has done nothing.
strings.feedbackThinVerdict: Those facts are a good start. A conclusion about a person does not belong in the report, so take those picks out. Then add a couple more of the things you saw yourself.
strings.mustRemoveConclusion: Take the conclusion out before you finish. A report holds what you saw yourself, not what you think it means. Having a theory is normal; it belongs with the people whose job it is to look into it.
